lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Did you notice how differently the new manager treats Marek?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Yeah — she's giving him way more responsibility this month, ever since she found out he used to run his own startup.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Right, and he's clearly working harder because of it. It's like he's trying to prove she's right about him.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: That's exactly the Pygmalion effect we read about. She expects a lot from him, so he performs better.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Meanwhile, she barely talks to the new intern. He probably notices that too.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Definitely. People usually sense these things, even when nobody says anything out loud.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: So expectations really do shape behaviour, not just talent.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Seems that way. I'm rethinking how I talk to my own team now, honestly.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Did you read that article about how the placebo effect was actually discovered?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Yeah — a nurse gave a soldier salt water because they'd run out of morphine, right?

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Exactly. And while Beecher was reviewing all those old trial records years later, he kept finding the same pattern everywhere.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: That's wild. So he wasn't even looking for it originally?

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: No, he was just investigating something completely different when he noticed it.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: It's funny how some of the biggest discoveries happened while someone was doing something else entirely.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Definitely. Makes you wonder what we're missing right now, while we're focused on something totally different.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Now I'm slightly worried about what I overlooked this week.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Have you ever felt like you don't actually deserve your job, even though everyone says you're doing great?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Constantly, actually. I read that psychologists coined a term for that back in 1978.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Right, impostor syndrome. Apparently interest in it has grown massively over the past decade.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: That doesn't surprise me. I've definitely felt it more since I got promoted last year.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Same here. I joined this team in January and I still sometimes think they made a mistake hiring me.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Have you told anyone that?

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Not until just now, actually.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Well, for what it's worth, you've clearly earned your spot.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Have you noticed that in most group projects, two people somehow end up doing all the work?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Constantly. I've actually been reading about exactly why that happens — it's called social loafing.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Oh, I think I've heard of that — some old rope-pulling experiment?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Exactly. A French engineer called Ringelmann discovered it back in 1913.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: So has anyone actually found a fix for it?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Sort of. Teams that track everyone's contribution separately have counteracted it pretty well.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: I've been trying that with my own team lately, actually.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: And has it worked?

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Did you know that guy who robbed banks with lemon juice on his face actually believed it made him invisible?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Ha, yes — I read about that. Apparently he'd seen something about lemon juice being used as invisible ink.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Right, and he'd reasoned that it would work on cameras too, which obviously it didn't.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: That's basically how the Dunning-Kruger effect got its name, isn't it?

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Yeah — the psychologists had already noticed the same pattern in much smaller ways before that story even came out.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Like people who do worst on a test rating themselves the most confident?

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Exactly. They'd been seeing that in their own classroom data for a while.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Kind of comforting, actually — means the people who worry they're bad at something probably aren't.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Are you worried about AI taking over your job at some point?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Honestly, a bit. I think a lot of routine tasks will disappear eventually.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Same here. My company's actually launching a whole new automated system next month.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Wait, seriously? Is that going to affect your team directly?

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Probably, yeah. That's why I've decided — I'm going to start a coding course next week.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Good plan. I'll probably look into something similar myself, actually.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: We're meeting the training provider on Friday, if you want to join.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Definitely — count me in.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Be honest — do you actually think we'll finish this on time?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Realistically? By the deadline, we'll probably still be fixing bugs.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: That's exactly the planning fallacy we read about, isn't it?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Pretty much. We always assume nothing will go wrong this time.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: So what if we actually built in a proper buffer for once?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Honestly, by the time we double the estimate, we'll probably have gotten it about right.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: This time next month, I'd rather already have shipped it than still be apologising for the delay.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Same. Let's actually plan for the unexpected this time.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: How was your trip to the Tokyo office?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Really interesting, actually. You have to ask permission for almost everything there — even small things.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Really? Here you can just go ahead and decide yourself, mostly.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Exactly. I wasn't able to just email a client directly without looping in my manager first.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: That sounds exhausting, but I guess it avoids mistakes.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Maybe. Though honestly, you don't have to over-explain every little decision here, and I kind of missed that.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Could you get used to working like that long-term?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Probably, but I definitely prefer having more autonomy.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Do you actually believe you can tell when someone's lying just by watching them?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Honestly, not really. We just read an article saying crossed arms and eye contact barely mean anything.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Right, that surprised me too. I always assumed avoiding eye contact must mean someone's guilty.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Apparently not — liars might actually hold more eye contact, not less.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: So if my colleague seems really calm and confident, that doesn't mean she's telling the truth.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Exactly. She could just be a good liar, or she could genuinely be telling the truth — you can't really tell from that alone.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: So what actually works, then?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Apparently, checking if their story stays consistent matters way more than how they're standing.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Honestly, looking back, I think we should have tested this feature more before launch.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Maybe, but at the time nobody flagged it as risky — it's easy to say that now.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: True. I guess that's exactly the hindsight bias thing we just read about.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Right — we could have caught it earlier, sure, but we genuinely didn't have the information back then.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Still, the client shouldn't have found out about the bug from a tweet before we even told them.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Yeah, that part's fair. We definitely should have communicated faster.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Given how quiet the dev team's been all morning, they must have been dealing with it since last night.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Probably. Let's actually judge this properly instead of just blaming everyone in hindsight.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Did you know some countries flipped organ donation to opt-out, and consent rates went through the roof?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Yeah, I read about that. Nothing was forced — the default was just changed.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: It's wild how much a tiny design choice can shape behaviour.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Apparently the same trick's been used in loads of places — like that fly thing in the Amsterdam urinals.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Right, the spillage was cut by something like 80%, just from one image.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Honestly, I think a version of that could be introduced here at work too.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Like what, exactly?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Making the healthy snack the default option in the vending machine, instead of hiding it behind three buttons.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: That Milgram study is genuinely unsettling. It's believed to have actually tested obedience, not memory at all.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Right — the whole 'memory and learning' cover story was just deception from the start.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: I keep thinking about how few people actually walked away, even when they were clearly distressed.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Honestly, I'd like to think I'd have refused, but who really knows.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Anyway — completely different topic, I'm getting my boiler serviced this weekend.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Good idea before winter properly hits. Did you have someone recommended?

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Yeah, a neighbour had hers fixed last month and said the engineer was great.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: One thing's for sure — I'd never just blindly follow instructions like that, no matter who was giving them.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Honestly, that loss aversion reading hit a little close to home.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Same. I always hold onto a losing stock way longer than I should, hoping it'll recover.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Exactly the disposition effect they described. Meanwhile you'd sell a winner instantly.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Guilty. What about you — got anything you're watching right now?

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Actually yes. If it drops another five percent, I'll sell it before it gets any worse.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: See, that's the rational move. I just never manage to actually do it.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: It's funny — if you frame it as avoiding a loss instead of missing a gain, people take way more risks.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Which explains basically every 'last chance' advert I've ever fallen for.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: If I had unlimited savings, I'd honestly quit tomorrow and travel for a year.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Same, though I'd probably get bored after about three months.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: What about your feared self, going by that possible-selves thing we read about?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Honestly? Still doing exactly this job in ten years, having never once tried anything new.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: That's a genuinely vivid image, not just a vague worry.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Yeah, it actually made me a bit uncomfortable, if I'm honest.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Good — if you pictured it even more clearly, you'd probably feel more motivated to actually change something.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Fair. Maybe that's exactly the point of the exercise.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Didn't you take some kind of certification course last year that you weren't enjoying?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Oh, don't remind me. I kept going for another six months after I knew it wasn't for me.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: If you'd quit the moment you realised, you would have saved a lot of time and money.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Exactly. But I'd already paid for it, so quitting felt like throwing that money away.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Classic sunk cost thinking, though — the money was already gone either way.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: I know that now. At the time it just felt like giving up.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: If I'd been there, I would have told you the fee was gone regardless of what you chose next.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Fair. I'd probably have listened too — eventually.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Honestly, I still think about that Berlin job sometimes.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: The one you turned down? If you'd taken it, you'd be living abroad right now.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Exactly. Completely different life, probably.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: I get it. If I weren't so indecisive, I'd have applied for that course years ago.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: You still could, though — that one's not exactly closed forever.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: True. It's a bit like that reading, isn't it — focusing on the near miss instead of what's actually in front of you.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: The silver medallist thing? Yeah, exactly. Always comparing to the gold they narrowly missed.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Maybe I should start comparing to fourth place instead.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Honestly, I wish I had travelled more before starting my career.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Same. Once you're settled, it's so much harder to just go.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Speaking of things I wish were different — I wish you would stop leaving dishes in my sink.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Fair. That one's genuinely on me, not just a wish.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: It's funny, actually, after that reading — I don't think I'll regret this conversation in twenty years.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: No, but you might regret not travelling more, based on what we read.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Exactly. Apparently regret over things we never tried just lasts a lot longer.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Noted. I should probably stop putting off that trip I keep talking about, then.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: My colleague called this morning about the meeting.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Oh yeah? What did she say?

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: She said it had been moved to Thursday, not Wednesday.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Good thing she called. Did you ask her anything?

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Yeah, I asked whether I needed to prepare anything.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: And?

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: She asked me to bring the quarterly figures, that's it.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Easy enough. Glad she caught the date change.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Something weird happened on my street this morning.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: What happened?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: A woman dropped all her shopping bags, and honestly, nobody moved for a good ten seconds.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Ten seconds is a long time. Did someone eventually help?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Yeah, the woman who was walking a dog finally stopped and helped her pick everything up.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: That's exactly what we just read about — diffusion of responsibility.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Right, everyone probably assumed someone else would step in first.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: At least someone finally did. That's the reassuring part.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: You still haven't replied to that email, have you?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: I keep avoiding opening it. I know that's ridiculous.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: It's not ridiculous, it's just what we read about — you're avoiding the feeling, not the task itself.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: That's fair. It's just such an aversive thing to deal with right now.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Try setting a timer for five minutes and just starting. You don't have to finish it.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Five minutes I can manage. Okay, I'll try doing that after this.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Good. Let me know how it goes.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: I will — oh, and I forgot to say, thanks for the advice.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: I've been standing here for ten minutes and I still can't pick a phone.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: There are, what, thirty models on this wall? No wonder.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Exactly. They all look basically the same to me at this point.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Try picking two or three must-have features and ignoring everything else.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Good battery life, a decent camera, and that's genuinely it?

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: That's it. Anything beyond that is just noise at this point.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: This is exactly that paradox of choice thing we read about, isn't it.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Word for word. Now go pick one before we're here all afternoon.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: We launched that feature without proper testing last month, and it broke almost immediately.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Did nobody flag that during the review meeting?

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: Honestly, I think everyone assumed someone else already had concerns and had raised them.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: That sounds exactly like the groupthink thing we just read about.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: It really does. Nobody wanted to be the one slowing things down.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: Maybe assign someone to deliberately argue against the plan next time.

lines.speaker: Tomasz
lines.line: A formal devil's advocate. I like that.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.line: It sounds awkward, but arguably it's exactly what would have caught this.

l21Articles.text: It took an hour to arrive.
She used to be an MP.
